script:
Solving lighting challenges when using a Deep Winter colour palette

[warmly] Okay — so you've got this gorgeous deep winter colour palette… sapphire blues, emerald greens, rich charcoals… and somehow, once the lights go on, it just FALLS flat.

Here's the thing — it's not your colours at all… it's your LIGHTING. And the fix is simpler than you'd think.

Natural light is honestly your best friend with a deep winter palette — especially that cool, soft light from a NORTH-facing window… it just reveals all that depth.

A little tip I love: sheer curtains or blinds to diffuse direct sunlight — keeps the room bright without flattening those intense jewel tones, you know?

Layering your lighting is what really makes the difference — overhead lights alone will FLATTEN everything… you need ambient, task, and accent lights working together.

[excited] Honestly, one of my favourites — LED strips hidden behind floating shelves near a navy feature wall… the way it plays with shadow and light is just stunning.

Now — balancing COOL and warm tones is where it gets interesting… you don't want it icy, but you don't want those cool hues going muddy either.

When it comes to FIXTURES — choose finishes that actually work with your palette… brushed nickel, matte black, or dark bronze all sit beautifully with deep winter tones.

And avoid warm yellow bulbs if you can — they'll dull your blues and greens… aim for around 4000K to 5000K for that crisp, clear light that keeps the palette VIBRANT.

[gently] For dim spaces, mirrors are honestly a game-changer — bounce natural light into darker corners and spread that glow right across your deep winter palette.

Reflective surfaces — think lacquered side tables or metallic accessories — do the same thing… they catch and MULTIPLY the light without adding any extra fittings.

Okay — lumens vs watts… lumens tell you how BRIGHT a bulb actually is, watts just tell you how much energy it uses — so always check lumens when shopping.

Light PLACEMENT matters so much — a downlight aimed at a charcoal wall will look completely different to a lamp positioned low and to the side… experiment a little.

Wall art is where accent lighting REALLY earns its keep — a small picture light or directional spot makes your prints look like they belong in a gallery, trust me.

Floor and table lamps are brilliant for adding warmth at lower levels — they stop the space feeling TOO cool or clinical when you've got a lot of deep, bold tones going on.

And this is one I come back to all the time — a well-placed lamp can completely SHIFT the mood… from bright and energising in the morning, to soft and intimate by evening.

Dimmers and smart lighting let you ADAPT the mood throughout the day — crank up the clarity for daytime, then let those blues and greens shimmer under low light at night.

[softly] And honestly… there's something really lovely about using soft, layered light in a deep winter room for winding down — it genuinely affects how CALM the space feels.

So to sum it up — aim for 4000K to 5000K bulbs, LAYER your lighting, use natural light smartly, and let accent lights do the heavy lifting for your wall art and deep winter tones.

Pro tip — matte and satin wall finishes actually soften the intensity of your deep winter palette beautifully under layered lighting… way more forgiving than high gloss.

And if you want wall art that actually WORKS with a deep winter palette and all this beautiful lighting… we've got sets over on About Wall Art that are made for exactly this.
